extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of political economy; economists and policymakers interested in precise definitions of economic categories
extracted.subtask_description: Clarifying the proper economic definitions and boundaries of the abstract terms 'wages', 'wealth', and 'capital', and diagnosing common confusions in their use so as to enable correct reasoning about distribution and production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of wages
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages means the return received for the exertion of labor, as distinguished from the return received for the use of capital, and the return received by the landholder for the use of land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes all earnings that are the result or reward of exertion: the self-employing gold-digger's washed gold, the hunter's game, the fisherman's fish, and the portion of retail storekeepers' profits that recompense their labor rather than capital. Keep this broad economic sense in mind even when narrower common meanings are used elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adam Smith's definition of capital
rubrics_metrics.description: "That part of a man's stock which he expects to afford him a revenue is called his capital." (Adam Smith) — the capital of a country consists of: (1) machines and instruments of trade; (2) buildings not mere dwellings; (3) improvements of land; (4) acquired and useful abilities of inhabitants; (5) money; (6) provisions in hands of producers/dealers expected to yield profit; (7) material or partially completed manufactured articles; (8) completed articles in hands of producers/dealers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith further distinguishes the first four as fixed capital and the last four as circulating capital. His inclusion of personal qualities is noted as a slip; use his core idea that capital is stock expected to yield revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ricardo's definition of capital
rubrics_metrics.description: "Capital is that part of the wealth of a country which is employed in production, and consists of food, clothing, tools, raw materials, machinery, etc., necessary to give effect to labor."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ricardo's definition emphasizes items actually employed in production and thus excludes certain items Adam Smith would include (e.g., acquired talents). It risks excluding stocks of luxury goods or merchant inventories not used in production.

rubrics_metrics.name: McCulloch's definition of capital
rubrics_metrics.description: "The capital of a nation really comprises all those portions of the produce of industry existing in it that may be directly employed either to support human existence or to facilitate production."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wider than Ricardo's: includes anything capable of aiding production regardless of actual use. Example/anti-pattern: this makes a pleasure carriage horse capital because it could be used to draw a plow—thus including things capable of but not actually used in production.

rubrics_metrics.name: John Stuart Mill's definition of capital
rubrics_metrics.description: "Whatever things are destined to supply productive labor with the shelter, protection, tools and materials which the work requires, and to feed and otherwise maintain the laborer during the process, are capital."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mill uses the owner's intention/destination to determine capital status. This makes the criterion subjective: whether the owner intends to devote items to productive labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wayland's two senses of capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital is used in two senses: (a) in relation to product, any substance on which industry is to be exerted; (b) in relation to industry, the material on which industry is about to confer value, including instruments used for conferring value and means of sustenance of the worker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes perspective-dependent senses — be explicit whether you mean 'in relation to product' or 'in relation to industry' when classifying items as capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflating capital with labor or land (exclude human powers and natural supplies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Human powers, whether natural or acquired (knowledge, skill, industry), and things freely supplied by nature (land, natural forces) should not be classed as capital in exact economic reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are common metaphorical uses that must be eschewed for precise analysis. Example anti-patterns: calling a man's knowledge his capital; counting natural land or a falling stream itself as capital rather than as land or natural opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common-sense definition of capital (wealth devoted to procuring more wealth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital is wealth devoted to procuring more wealth: 'that part of a man's stock which he expects to afford him revenue is called his capital.' The capital of a community is the sum of such individual stocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this functional/common understanding when practical conclusions are drawn; it aligns with ordinary usage outside pedantic definitional disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of wealth (political economy sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth consists of natural products that have been secured, moved, combined, separated, or otherwise modified by human exertion so as to fit them for the gratification of human desires—i.e., labor impressed upon matter producing tangible things (buildings, cattle, tools, machinery, products).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude things that merely have exchange value but do not change aggregate wealth (bonds, mortgages, bank bills, debts, slaves as instruments of appropriation, or land values that represent transfers). Wealth must be tangible products whose production increases aggregate wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital vs. wealth distinction: capital is only part of wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: All capital is wealth, but not all wealth is capital. Capital is that part of wealth devoted to the aid of production (wealth in course of exchange), whereas other wealth may be held for direct consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify items by purpose/use: e.g., stock of a merchant or materials held for sale are capital; personal possessions or consumables in the hands of consumers are not. Examples given: a tailor's coat made for sale is capital; a coat made for self is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: capital as 'wealth in course of exchange'
rubrics_metrics.description: Capital can be defined as 'wealth in course of exchange', where 'exchange' includes passing from hand to hand and transmutations when natural reproductive/transforming forces are utilized for increase of wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This captures tools, merchant stock, infrastructure placed in service of many users (railroads, telegraph lines, hotels). It excludes wealth kept in hands of direct consumers (homestead, private amusements). Example: a manufacturer's lathe used to make saleable goods is capital; a gentleman's lathe for amusement is not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-term caution in economic reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms like 'wealth', 'capital', 'wages' are abstract; nothing can be generally affirmed or denied of them that cannot be affirmed or denied of the whole class they represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid fallacies that arise from treating specific instances as if they justified general statements about the abstract class. Remember exchangeability is intrinsic to the economic idea of wealth/capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wages are produced by labor, not always drawn from capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The produce of labor constitutes the natural recompense or wages of labor. In simple cases where laborers are self-employing or paid in kind, wages clearly result directly from labor and are not drawn from capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrations: gathering eggs/berries, making shoes (wages are the finished product), share-tenancy/metayer systems, 'lay' payment on whaling ships (share of catch). Therefore, blanket premises that 'wages are drawn from capital' are overbroad: at most, only some wages (those paid by employers) may be drawn from capital. Do not assume the universal truth that wages come from capital when reasoning about distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use possession/intended use as practical test for capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether an item of wealth is capital depends practically on whether it is in the possession of the consumer or is in course of exchange/possession of someone who intends it for production/exchange.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If wealth is held by a consumer for direct gratification (food in housewife's pantry, a toy of a child), it is not capital; if held in stock for sale or to support production (food in a restaurant, merchant stock), it is capital. This pragmatic test often matches ordinary judgments about capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude relative/transferable claims from being counted as wealth in economic aggregates
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidences of debt (bonds, mortgages, notes, bank bills) and other transfer claims represent relative wealth between persons but do not increase aggregate wealth and thus should not be treated as wealth in the economic sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: canceling debts or emancipating slaves alters distribution, not aggregate wealth. Land values that reflect exclusive rights are transfers, not additions to common wealth; they should not be equated with wealth that adds to production.
